title: stochastic-warmup-schedule-and-benchmark-replay
body:
Purpose and scope:

This notebook-style design doc records a set of experiments and a lightweight harness for evaluating stochastic warmup schedules and replayable benchmark runs. The goal is to bracket the trade-offs between predictable throughput claims and run-to-run variance introduced by non-deterministic warmup procedures and runtime microstate drift (GPU caches, kernel scheduling, OS jitter). We want a repeatable methodology for: 1) producing stable throughput baselines, 2) quantifying uncertainty, and 3) enabling post-facto replay of specific runs for debugging and regression analysis.

Motivation (why different from our existing warmup playbooks):
- Many previous playbooks assume fixed-length, deterministic priming sequences. In realistic traffic, clients vary inter-arrival times, and the serving runtime adapts (batchers, prefetch). Deterministic priming sometimes underestimates variance and hides brittle operating points.
- We need an approach that intentionally injects controlled stochasticity into priming so that the harness observes realistic operating envelopes while preserving replayability.

Key definitions used in this doc:
- Warmup schedule: sequence of synthetic requests used to bring the system from cold to steady state.
- Checkpointing: capture of runtime-relevant artifacts (GPU mem usage, KV cache hashes, latency histograms, RNG seed) at named points so a run can be approximately rehydrated.
- Replay token: an identifier linking a recorded checkpoint and the random seed stream that produced the observed metrics.

High-level approach:
1) Generate an ensemble of warmup schedules drawn from a configurable stochastic policy (Poisson, bursty + geometric backoff, uniform jitter). Each schedule is parameterized and tagged.
2) For every schedule, run a short priming phase and then a benchmark window. Capture rich telemetry and create a checkpoint (metadata-only: seeds, config, observed microstate summaries).
3) Repeat each schedule N times (N >= 5) to estimate variance and build confidence intervals.
4) For any candidate run we want to debug later, use its checkpoint + seed to replay the same request timing and content to reproduce the GPU/serving microstate trajectory as closely as possible.

Experiment matrix and config knobs:
- Warmup duration: {short: 15s, medium: 60s, long: 300s}
- Inter-arrival distribution: {poisson (lambda), bursty (on-off with burst length distribution), fixed-interval with jitter}
- Burst intensity: {low, medium, high} controlling peak concurrency vs baseline
- Entropy source: deterministic seed vs hardware entropy (to measure seed sensitivity)
- Checkpoint frequency: {none, after-warmup, rolling-every-30s}
- Benchmark window: 60s stable window after warmup
- Repetitions: 5–10 per config cell

Measurements to collect per run (minimal required):
- aggregated throughput (tokens/sec, requests/sec) time series at 1s granularity
- P50/P90/P99 latency (generation and total request) time series
- GPU utilization and memory snapshot before/after warmup
- Batch size distribution observed by runtime
- Kernel selection log (if available) and quantization path used
- RNG seed and client-side timestamp sequence used for request arrival and payload sampling
- Minor OS-level noise indicators: CPU steal, context switch rate, IRQ counts (if available)
- A small deterministic sample of outputs (hashes) for content-stability checks

Checkpointing model (lightweight metadata-only approach):
- We do not persist full GPU RAM images. Instead capture: 1) a compact microstate summary (hashes and counters for KV cache, slot occupancy, tail micro-batch sizes), 2) RNG master seed and the schedule random seed, 3) loader offset pointers (if using corpus sampling), 4) exact versions of runtime binary and CUDA/cuDNN/cuBLAS versions.
- Format: key-value YAML-like block stored as part of run artifacts. Each checkpoint is named with a UUID and stored in artifact storage with a replay manifest.

Replay strategy to approximate the original run:
- Rehydrate the checkpoint metadata (seeds, policy parameters, corpus offsets).
- Re-run a client harness that deterministically schedules requests and payload draws using the seeds.
- Disable non-deterministic fallback features (where possible) in the runtime: autoscale-triggered resharding, ephemeral logging-induced backpressure, ephemeral telemetry sinks.
- Replay expectation: we expect microstate divergence within a bounded envelope. Use the recorded sample-output hashes to assert content equivalence where semantics permit.

Acceptance criteria for stable throughput baseline:
- For a claimed steady-state throughput T, 95% of repeated runs (for the same schedule cell) should produce throughput in [0.95*T, 1.05*T] during the benchmark window, with P99 latency below the SLO for the plan.
- If variance exceeds threshold, record the schedule cell as high-variance and include it in the stochastic regression suite.

Practical harness implementation notes (client-side):
- Client harness exposes a small DSL for warmup policies. Example policy record: {"policy": "poisson", "lambda": 20 rps, "burst_prob": 0.1, "burst_multiplier": 4, "jitter": 0.2}. The harness serializes policy+seed into the run manifest.
- Use a local high-resolution timer and pre-generated arrival timestamps to avoid client-side scheduling jitter. Pre-generate timestamps in a single-threaded preparatory step and store them as an array indexed by request index.
- Payload selection should use reservoir sampling with a fixed seed to guarantee the same corpus draws on replay.

Example minimal warmup pseudo-configs (text form for the run manifest):
- short-poisson-seed-42: {warmup: 15s, policy: poisson, lambda: 50 rps, seed: 42, checkpoint: after-warmup}
- long-bursty-seed-1729: {warmup: 300s, policy: bursty, base: 10 rps, burst_prob: 0.2, burst_mult: 8, seed: 1729, checkpoint: rolling-30s}

Quick diagnostic checklist when reproducibility fails:
- Confirm runtime versions and kernel versions match the checkpoint. Small driver shifts can change kernel selection heuristics and cause divergence.
- Verify the RNG seeds were set and consumed deterministically (some client libraries fetch extra randomness on first call). Add a deterministic call to the RNG at harness startup to align sequence numbers.
- Check if autoscaler or background host activity introduced extra queues; turn off autoscaling for replay runs.
- Inspect batch-size distribution logs: if distribution changed, look for differences in arrival timestamps or client pacing accuracy.

Reporting and artifact capture:
- The harness should produce a single run record JSON (separate from checkpoint metadata) containing run_id, schedule_id, policy, seed, backend image digest, measured metrics (aggregate and time-series compacted), and links to telemetry traces.
- Tag runs with labels: controlled-priming | stochastic-priming | replayable | high-variance so downstream dashboards can filter.

Follow-ups and experiments to run next:
- Measure sensitivity to GPU microstate by perturbing small allocator sizes pre-warmup and observing throughput envelope shifts.
- Evaluate impact of deterministic vs hardware entropy seeds on output quality (hash checks) and latency variance.
- Correlate batcher window parameters with variance under high-burst policies; tune batching latency knobs for worst-case stability.

Open questions / risks:
- How close can a metadata-only checkpoint get us to full microstate replay? We need empirical bounds; plan experiments where we intentionally diverge a single microstate variable and measure effect size.
- Operationally, rolling checkpoint frequency increases artifact volume; strike a balance between observability and storage costs.

Appendix: minimal client pseudo-step for replayable schedules
1) Initialize harness with manifest (policy + seed + corpus-seed).
2) Pre-generate arrival timestamps and payload indices using the provided seeds.
3) Warmup: emit requests following the pre-generated schedule.
4) At checkpoint points, persist microstate summary and captured metrics.
5) Run benchmark window with same schedule and collect time-series.

Notes to self: keep the first rollout small (3 schedule families x 3 durations x 5 repetitions) to get a quick signal before expanding. Store sample outputs (small hashes) for one deterministic prompt set to validate semantic stability.

If the team finds these ideas useful, I'll convert the notebook into a small harness Python package (client harness + manifest writer) and wire it to our existing run recorder.
